doc.title: Dick Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Forming the Catatonic Five, bourbon pay and the pizza story
summary: Having heard the Fallacious Five jam, he formed his own band with Emerson Brown, Derry Hall and others, paid in bourbon; a Deke House gig ends with a pizza and Emerson's anchovy remark.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Silliman Hall. And the band at that time was Bob Krompart on cornet, Collier on trombone, John Fell was the clarinetist, the pianist was Pete Zeeveld, and Mike Beldock, who had a distinguished career as an attorney and still does, was the drummer in the band. And anyway I used to just sit there with my freshman beanie on and listen to these old men.

They seemed so old to me. They tolerated my presence with my beanie, and then they graduated. And so I decided I’ll form my own band. So it took me a year or two to round up the co-founders. I got Emerson Brown and Derry Hall. Derry Hall was a pianist and a guitarist. But as it turned out we needed a trombonist so he taught himself trombone. And we had Ron Jabaul of the Alpha Del house, he was the cornetist, Dave Barbour was at Theta Del, he was the pianist, and his only failing was that he had to read music. And he was the only one in the band that could read music, and he needed the music. And you talked a bit about alcohol before, and we were all pretty heavy drinkers. And when we played a gig we were never paid in cash in those days, this was early fifties, ’50, ’51, ’52. And by ’52 we had a good solid band and everybody got paid when we had a gig, of a quart of bourbon.

It was cheaper, and it was Blue Chip Bourbon as I recall. And in that band we had Emerson Brown of course, Derry Hall, let’s see Derry Hall was playing trombone in that band then. And the band played an exhausting gig at the Deke House and we all fell asleep under the piano. And we awoke several hours later, and I knew they would be hungry. I was the leader of the band so I felt responsible for giving them vittles, and that’s another Emerson Brown story, he was snoring along with the rest of them so I decided to go down to Clinton, get a pizza pie, I got two big pies, brought it back, shoved it under the piano and started to kick the soles of their feet, and they said, “Oh my goodness, that smells wonderful, this is terrific, what a smell to wake up to.” Everybody was so thankful and appreciative of my initiative in getting this pie, except for Emerson. Emerson’s response, and I can remember that after fifty years was, “What, no anchovies?” That’s Emerson.
